chordCategoryDescriptions.open: First-position chords that use [[openChord|open strings]] — the shapes every guitarist learns first.
chordCategoryDescriptions.triad: Three-note chords, or [[triad|triads]]. [[major|Major]] (1–3–5) sounds bright, [[minor|minor]] (1–♭3–5) sounds sad.
chordCategoryDescriptions.sus: The [[third|3rd]] is replaced by the 2nd (sus2) or 4th (sus4). Neither major nor minor, so it sounds unresolved.
chordCategoryDescriptions.sixth: A [[triad|triad]] with an added 6th or 9th — but no 7th.
chordCategoryDescriptions.seventh: A triad with a [[seventh|7th]] on top. The core colour of jazz, blues and funk.
chordCategoryDescriptions.extended: [[seventhChord|Seventh chords]] with the 9th, 11th or 13th ([[extension|extensions]]) stacked on top. On guitar some notes, usually the 5th, are left out.
chordCategoryDescriptions.power: Just the [[root|root]] and [[fifth|fifth]] (1–5). With no 3rd it is neither major nor minor. The backbone of rock and metal.
chordCategoryDescriptions.slash: In a [[slashChord|slash chord]] (C/E) the note after the slash is played in the bass. The chord stays the same, only the lowest note changes — an [[inversion|inversion]]. That smooths the bass line: C – G/B – Am.

diatonic.title: Chords in the key
diatonic.description: The [[diatonic|diatonic]] chord built on each [[degree|degree]] of the scale. Most songs are made of these.

detector.title: Chord finder
detector.description: Click one fret per string; click it again to clear it. The finder names the chord your notes make.
detector.unknown: These notes don't form a known chord.

mobility.title: Movable and fixed shapes
mobility.movableHint: No open strings. Slide the shape along the neck and you get the same chord type from another root: every [[fret|fret]] is a [[semitone|semitone]].
mobility.fixedHint: [[openChord|Open strings]] ring, so the shape only gives this chord right here. Move it to another fret and the chord changes.
mobility.slideHint: Slide a movable shape one fret up and you get {{up}}, one fret down and you get {{down}}. Twelve frets up it is {{twelve}} again.

slash.explain: This is a {{chord}} chord, but the lowest note is {{bass}} ({{degree}} from the root).

inversions.0: The bass is not a chord tone, so it adds extra colour.
inversions.1: This is the first [[inversion|inversion]]: the [[third|third]] is in the bass.
inversions.2: This is the second [[inversion|inversion]]: the [[fifth|fifth]] is in the bass.
inversions.3: This is the third [[inversion|inversion]]: the [[seventh|seventh]] is in the bass.

slash.inversionsHint: The same chord with another chord tone in the bass — an [[inversion|inversion]]. Used to walk the bass line step by step.

progressions.description: Three steps: pick a [[key|key]], pick a [[progression|progression]], then click any chord to change it. The colours show what each chord does in the progression — its [[harmonicFunction|function]].
progressions.editHint: Click any chord to see what else could go in its place.
progressions.howToRead: How to read ([[romanNumerals|Roman numerals]]): capital letters (I, IV, V) are [[major|major]] chords, lower case (ii, vi) [[minor|minor]], ° [[diminished|diminished]]. "/3" means the third is in the bass (a [[slashChord|slash chord]]).

functionHints.tonic: stable, feels like home. Progressions usually end here.
functionHints.subdominant: moves away from home and creates motion.
functionHints.dominant: builds tension; the ear wants to go back to the tonic.

key.title: Swap for another chord
key.hint: The 7 [[diatonic|diatonic]] chords of the key. Any of them fits here.

colour.title: Change the colour
colour.hint: Same [[root|root]], different sound: maj7 is soft, [[sus|sus]] is suspended, add9 is bright.

bass.title: Change the bass note
bass.hint: Same chord, different lowest note (a [[slashChord|slash chord]]). The bass line moves smoothly.

outside.title: Outside the key
outside.hint: Bolder choices: [[secondaryDominant|secondary dominants]] and [[borrowedChord|chords borrowed]] from the parallel key.

sourceHints.secondary: V7/x: pulls strongly to the next chord

keyTable.title: Chords in the key
keyTable.hint: [[diatonic|Diatonic]] chords built on each scale degree. Click one to add it to the end of the progression.

hint.major: Common "outside" chords in major: [[secondaryDominant|secondary dominants]] and chords borrowed from the [[parallelKey|parallel minor]] (iv, ♭VI, ♭VII…).
hint.minor: Common "outside" chords in minor: the major V from [[harmonicMinor|harmonic minor]], [[secondaryDominant|secondary dominants]] and chords borrowed from the [[parallelKey|parallel major]].

presetHints.pop: The most used progression of the last 20 years, found in thousands of pop songs.
presetHints.threeChord: The backbone of rock'n'roll and folk: [[tonic|tonic]], [[subdominant|subdominant]], [[dominant|dominant]].
presetHints.jazzTwoFiveOne: The core jazz cadence: each [[seventhChord|seventh chord]] moves down a [[fifth|fifth]] to the next.
presetHints.sensitive: The pop progression starting on the minor chord; it sounds sadder.
presetHints.royalRoad: A favourite of Japanese pop and anime music.
presetHints.canon: The bass walks down step by step. [[slashChord|Slash chords]] make that possible.
presetHints.descendingBass: The chords change while the bass steps down each time. Common in ballads and rock.
presetHints.mixolydianRock: The ♭VII chord in major, a [[borrowedChord|borrowed chord]]. The sound of classic rock.
presetHints.blues: The classic 12-bar blues form; every chord is a dominant 7th.
presetHints.minorBasic: The three main chords of minor: i, iv, v.
presetHints.epic: A powerful progression, common in film and game music.
presetHints.minorRock: A minor progression for rock and metal.
presetHints.andalusian: The sound of flamenco: each chord steps down, ending on the major V from [[harmonicMinor|harmonic minor]].
presetHints.minorTwoFiveOne: The jazz cadence in minor: half-diminished ii, dominant V.
presetHints.circle: The chords walk around the circle of fifths. Common in jazz standards.
presetHints.dramatic: The major V at the end builds strong tension and leads back home.
presetHints.lineCliche: The chord stays put while one note in the bass falls by half steps.

solo.title: Solo map
solo.hint: Notes to solo with: the [[scale|scale]] ({{scale}}) in the background, the selected chord’s own notes on top. Landing on chord tones is the safest bet. While the progression plays, the map follows the chords.

roles.outside: not in the scale, use over this chord only

song.description: Type a song’s chords: the site finds its [[key|key]], explains what each chord does, moves it to any key you like and shows the easiest [[capo|capo]] position.
song.placeholder: For example: G Em C D  or  Am | F | C | G/B
song.unknown: These weren’t recognised as chords and were skipped: {{tokens}}
song.simplified: {{from}} isn’t in the catalogue and was analysed as {{to}}.
song.empty: Type the chords above and the site does the rest.

key.label: Key
key.share: {{inKey}} of {{count}} different chords belong to the key.
key.relative: {{first}} and {{second}} use the same notes: they are [[relativeKey|relative keys]]. The real key is the chord where the song feels at home, usually the one it ends on.

fitHints.harmonic: comes from minor with a raised 7th and pulls hard to the tonic.
fitHints.blues: a dominant 7th on I or IV of a major key. The core sound of the blues.
fitHints.secondary: the dominant of another chord in the key; it pulls strongly towards it.
fitHints.borrowed: taken from the parallel major/minor for a different colour.
fitHints.outside: fits none of the usual explanations: maybe a modulation or a special effect.

transpose.label: New key
transpose.capoInstead: Don’t want new shapes? Play the original chords with a [[capo|capo]] on fret {{count}}: it sounds the same.

capo.hint: Where to put a capo to play in {{key}}. Options are ranked by how many chords become open shapes.
capo.diagramsNote: Diagrams are relative to the capo: at fret {{count}} it becomes the new nut, and fret 1 on the diagram is the first fret above it.

builder.description: Build a chord yourself: pick a [[root|root]], then add or change degrees one at a time. The name, notes, sound and place on the neck update with every step.
builder.unnamedHint: This combination has no name in the catalogue, but it can still sound good.
builder.noDiagram: There is no diagram for this chord. Its notes are on the neck below.
builder.diagramWithFifth: The shape in the diagram includes the fifth.

ladder.title: Tower of thirds
ladder.hint: A chord is built by stacking [[third|thirds]] on the [[root|root]]: 1, 3, 5, 7, 9, 11, 13. Each floor sits about a third above the one below.

change.title: What did that change?
change.empty: Change any degree and I’ll explain what happened here.

third.none: You removed the third: the chord is neither major nor minor. With only root and fifth left it is a power chord.
third.3m: Minor third (♭3): the chord turned minor and darker.
third.3M: Major third (3): the chord turned major and brighter.
third.2M: The 2nd instead of the third (sus2): open, floating sound.
third.4P: The 4th instead of the third (sus4): tense, the ear waits for the third to return.

fifth.none: You dropped the fifth. Guitarists do it all the time: the fifth doesn’t change the chord’s name, it only adds body.
fifth.5d: Diminished fifth (♭5): tense and restless. With a minor third it makes a diminished chord.
fifth.5P: Perfect fifth (5): the most stable interval, it gives the chord body.
fifth.5A: Augmented fifth (♯5): unstable, hanging in the air. This is an augmented chord.

seventh.none: No seventh: the chord sounds like a plain triad.
seventh.6M: The 6th instead of a seventh: a soft, old-school jazz colour.
seventh.7d: Diminished seventh (♭♭7): a diminished seventh chord, very tense and symmetrical.
seventh.7m: Minor seventh (♭7): with a major third it makes a dominant 7, with a minor third a minor 7.
seventh.7M: Major seventh (7): soft, dreamy jazz sound (maj7).

ninth.9m: ♭9: a very tense colour that strengthens a dominant’s pull to the tonic.
ninth.9M: The 9th: really the 2nd an octave higher. It adds a bright, rich colour.
ninth.9A: ♯9: the sound of the "Hendrix chord", as if major and minor third rang at once.

eleventh.11P: The 11th: the 4th an octave higher. It clashes with a major third, so it’s mostly used on minor chords.
eleventh.11A: ♯11: the Lydian colour, bright and floating on major chords.

thirteenth.13m: ♭13: a dark, tense colour, usually on dominant chords.
thirteenth.13M: The 13th: the 6th an octave higher. The rich colour of jazz dominants.

steps.0: Everything starts with one note, the [[root|root]]. No chord yet.
steps.1: We put a major [[third|third]] on top. These two notes already set the mood: major.
steps.2: Another third on top of the third — the [[fifth|fifth]]. 1 – 3 – 5: the {{name}} [[triad|triad]] is ready.
steps.3: We lowered the third a semitone (♭3). Only one note changed, and the chord turned [[minor|minor]]: {{name}}.
steps.4: One more third on top: ♭7. A four-note minor [[seventhChord|seventh chord]]: {{name}}.
steps.5: And another: the 9th. {{name}} is a rich, jazzy chord. You can keep stacking thirds.

steps.0: We start from a major triad: 1 – 3 – 5, that is {{name}}.
steps.1: Add a major [[seventh|seventh]] (7): {{name}}, soft and dreamy.
steps.2: Lower the seventh a semitone (♭7): {{name}}, the [[dominant|dominant]] seventh. Tense, it wants to move down a fifth.
steps.3: Lower the third too: {{name}}, a minor seventh. Calmer and darker.
steps.4: Lower the fifth (♭5): {{name}}, half-diminished. The ii chord of minor keys.
steps.5: Lower the seventh once more (♭♭7): {{name}}. All notes are the same distance apart — fully symmetrical.

steps.0: Back to a major triad: 1 – 3 – 5, that is {{name}}.
steps.1: The 4th instead of the third: {{name}}. The ear waits for the third to come back (a [[sus|sus chord]]).
steps.2: Now the 2nd instead of the third: {{name}}. Open, modern sound.
steps.3: The third is back with a 6th on top: {{name}}. An old jazz and swing colour.
steps.4: A 9th instead of the 6th, no seventh: {{name}}. A favourite in pop and on acoustic guitar.
steps.5: 6th and 9th together: {{name}}. A classic jazz ending chord.

intervals.description: Click any note on the neck: every [[interval|interval]] around it lights up in colour. On guitar intervals are just finger shapes — learn one once and move it anywhere.
intervals.clickHint: Click another note to make it the reference. The area shown is ±5 frets, an easy reach for the hand.
intervals.gbHint: Note: between the G and B strings there is a major third, not a fourth, so shapes crossing that pair shift by a fret. The table works this out for the chosen string.

circle.description: A map of all 12 keys. Click a key to see its [[keySignature|key signature]], notes and main chords — the chords light up side by side on the circle.

how.clockwise: Clockwise, each step is a [[fifth|fifth]] up and adds a sharp: C → G → D…
how.counter: Counter-clockwise, each step is a fourth up and adds a flat: C → F → B♭…
how.neighbours: Neighbouring keys differ by just one note. Songs most easily move (modulate) to a neighbour.
how.inner: The inner ring holds the [[relativeKey|relative minor]]: Am uses the same notes as C major.
how.family: The six main chords of the selected key sit side by side: [[tonic|I]], [[subdominant|IV]] to its left, [[dominant|V]] to its right, and three minor chords underneath.

positions.label: Position
positions.title: Position {{n}}
positions.stretch: this position needs a wide stretch

systems.pentatonic: The scale splits into {{count}} positions with 2 notes per string. Each is a "box" where the hand stays put, and the boxes link up across the whole neck. Click a number.
systems.threePerString: The scale splits into {{count}} positions with 3 notes per string — an even layout that suits fast playing. Each position starts on a different degree. Click a number.
